strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: lightweight inference-time steering for both LLMs and VLMs without weight updates.
GRAINS combines contrastive Integrated Gradients, signed token selection, group-masking activation differences, PCA aggregation, and norm-preserving intervention into a coherent unified framework.

The empirical study is reasonably broad, covering two LLMs and three VLMs across truthfulness, toxicity, context faithfulness, hallucination, and visual preference alignment, with comparisons to LoRA and several strong steering baselines.

The reported target-task gains are substantial in several settings, including +13.22% on TruthfulQA for Llama-3.1-8B, a reduction in MMHal hallucination rate from 0.624 to 0.514 for LLaVA-1.6-7B, and +8.11% preference accuracy on SPA-VL.

The paper includes useful ablations on attribution method, visual versus textual attribution, and preference-based versus likelihood-based objectives, as well as qualitative examples and general-capability evaluations on MMLU/MMMU.
The method is presented clearly, and Figures 1 and 2 effectively communicate the conceptual differences from prior work and the three-stage GRAINS pipeline.
weaknesses: The claim that GRAINS operates without auxiliary supervision is misleading: it requires paired preferred and dispreferred responses to construct vectors. It avoids retraining, but not supervision or preference data.

The causal language is somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants. Integrated Gradients provides feature attribution under baseline and path assumptions, not automatically a causal effect; the signed component sum and masking choices also require stronger justification.

Several methodological details are underspecified, including sequence-logprob normalization and response-length effects, text and visual baselines, masking implementation, PCA centering and sign orientation, the final selected steering strengths, and which layers are intervened on.

Although token selection is token-sensitive, the resulting vector is applied globally to all token positions at inference. The paper should clarify that the intervention itself is not dynamically recomputed for each test input.

Experimental rigor is limited by the absence of variance estimates, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Some improvements over the strongest baselines are small and may not be statistically reliable.

There are numerical inconsistencies, especially for Toxigen: the base score is 51.19 in Table 1 but 48.10 in Table 6, while the text reports different gains of 7.79%, 9.79%, and 12.8%. These discrepancies must be reconciled.
The LoRA comparison may be weak because it uses only 50 examples and 10 iterations; the paper should justify that this is a competitive fine-tuning baseline or qualify the claimed advantage.

Reproducibility would be improved by a visible code/repository link, complete hyperparameter values, data-split sizes, random seeds, and clarification of the notation mismatch between λ in the method and α in the appendix.

The evaluation is concentrated on safety and hallucination tasks, and the preservation of general capabilities is only approximate rather than exact; broader out-of-domain and transfer evaluations would strengthen the central claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: lightweight inference-time control for both LLMs and VLMs without updating model weights.

The proposed pipeline is intuitive: contrastive Integrated Gradients identify influential tokens, masked inputs produce activation shifts, PCA aggregates those shifts, and the resulting vector is injected during inference.
The evaluation covers both language-only and multimodal settings, multiple safety-oriented objectives, and several strong steering and fine-tuning baselines.
The paper includes useful ablations on attribution method, vision versus text attribution, and preference-based versus single-reference objectives.
The reported construction overhead is low, and the preservation tests on MMLU and MMMU address an important concern of activation steering.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated or contradicted. The abstract says the method needs no auxiliary supervision, but the main procedure requires paired preferred and dispreferred responses. The method is also described as token-sensitive at inference, yet Equation 7 adds the same learned vector at every token position; token selection only affects offline vector construction.
The description of using two directions is misleading. Positive and negative effects are aggregated into one final vector v_l = v_l^+ - v_l^- and one additive intervention.

The PCA procedure has a fundamental sign and reproducibility problem: the sign of a first principal component is arbitrary for both v_l^+ and v_l^-. The paper does not state how the components are oriented before subtraction. It also omits PCA centering, explained variance, stability analysis, and cross-validation.

The neutral baselines used for Integrated Gradients and token masking are not specified, including whether text embeddings use zero vectors or mask embeddings and how visual-patch baselines are constructed. This is particularly important for VLMs.

The inference intervention is under-specified. The paper does not report the selected steering strengths for each model or task, whether all layers and positions are modified, random seeds, or the exact implementation of the normalization. The notation also changes from lambda in Equation 7 to alpha in the appendix.

Internal numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence. Toxigen base performance for Llama is 51.19 in Table 1 but 48.10 in Table 6. The text reports a 7.79% Toxigen gain for Llama, while Table 1 gives a 9.79% difference; the abstract says over 9.89%. Figure 1 reports VTI as -2.4% on SPA-VL, although Table 3 shows VTI improving over the base model for all three VLMs.
The claim that GRAINS achieves the lowest hallucination rate across all three VLM settings is not true for Qwen2.5-VL, where LoRA obtains 0.461 versus 0.473 for GRAINS.

The causal language is stronger than the evidence supports. Integrated Gradients is an attribution method, not a causal identification procedure. Validating selected tokens by ablating the same tokens used for selection is partly circular, and masked-token activation differences can reflect out-of-distribution context effects rather than clean semantic directions.

The empirical analysis lacks statistical rigor: results appear to be single runs with no confidence intervals, significance tests, variance across seeds, or robustness to different sampled steering sets. With only 50 construction examples per objective, stability is a major concern.

The LoRA comparison may not represent a strong fine-tuning baseline. The stated protocol uses only 10 iterations with a small learning rate, leaving unclear whether LoRA was converged or deliberately under-trained.

The metrics are confusing. Table 1 reports task accuracy while Table 4 reports BLEU accuracy on the same TruthfulQA benchmark, producing different base-model numbers without a clear explanation. BLEU-based similarity is also a weak proxy for fluency or semantic correctness, and no human evaluation is provided.

The contribution is somewhat incremental: it combines existing contrastive activation steering, Integrated Gradients, and PCA aggregation. The paper does not sufficiently establish broader impact beyond the limited set of safety and hallucination benchmarks.
The footnote labeled 'Code' contains no visible URL, and key implementation details needed for independent reproduction are missing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in inference-time control of LLMs and VLMs, offering a weight-update-free alternative that does not require external object detectors or auxiliary modules.

The method is intuitive and modular: it uses a contrastive preference objective, signed Integrated Gradients attributions, positive/negative token masking, per-layer PCA aggregation, and norm-preserving activation injection.

Empirical coverage is broad, spanning two LLM families and three VLM families across truthfulness, toxicity, faithfulness, hallucination, and visual safety tasks, with comparisons to LoRA and several strong steering baselines.

The paper evaluates side effects rather than only target-task accuracy, including MMLU, MMMU, generation-based BLEU metrics, inference throughput, cross-dataset transfer to RealToxicityPrompts and POPE, and numerous ablations.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful method diagrams, qualitative examples, attribution heatmaps, runtime information, prompts, and license details that support eventual reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: Integrated Gradients and contrastive activation steering with PCA are established techniques. The main contribution is their combination for attribution-guided vector construction and extension to multimodal tokens.

The description of GRAINS as selective or targeted token intervention is overstated. Attribution is used offline to construct one global steering vector per layer, while Equation 5 injects the same vector at every token position during decoding; it is not an instance-specific inference-time intervention on the selected tokens.

Several reproducibility-critical details are missing. In particular, PCA component signs are arbitrary, but no sign-orientation procedure is specified. The exact IG baseline for text and visual tokens, cross-modal attribution normalization, vector normalization, and task-specific lambda values are also not fully documented.

The experiments report only point estimates, with no random seeds, variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Since steering vectors are estimated from only 50 examples, the stability of the reported gains is unclear.

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies, such as the Toxigen base score of 51.19 in Table 1 versus 48.10 in Table 8, and the claimed 9.89-point Toxigen improvement in the text compared with a 9.79-point difference in Table 1. The relevant splits or rounding conventions should be clarified.

The claim that fluency is preserved is not directly supported: BLEU-based reference agreement is not a fluency metric, and no perplexity, human fluency evaluation, or broad open-ended linguistic-quality analysis is provided. The GPT-4o evaluation prompt and settings for MMHal-Bench are also omitted.

The causal interpretation of masked-token activation differences remains approximate. Group masking captures interactions and out-of-distribution baseline effects, while IG paths over discrete token or image-patch embeddings have known limitations. Attribution stability across seeds and baselines is not deeply analyzed.

The broad claim that GRAINS outperforms fine-tuning and prior methods should be qualified by the tested benchmarks and tuning protocol. Baseline hyperparameter tuning is not fully documented, and cross-dataset generalization is demonstrated on only one source-target pair for each behavior.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: lightweight inference-time steering of both LLMs and VLMs without weight updates, external detectors, or auxiliary modules.

GRAINS is conceptually coherent: signed Integrated Gradients attributions from a contrastive preference loss identify positive and negative tokens, masked contrastive hidden states yield layer-wise directions, PCA stabilizes those directions, and norm-preserving injection limits representation drift.
The empirical study is unusually broad, covering two LLMs, three VLMs, and a 72B-scale VLM across truthfulness, toxicity, context faithfulness, hallucination, and visual safety/alignment tasks.

GRAINS shows consistent average improvements over strong fine-tuning and activation-steering baselines, while largely preserving MMLU/MMMU performance and introducing less than 4% inference-time throughput overhead.

The paper includes many useful ablations: IG versus vanilla gradients, SmoothGrad, and random token selection; PCA versus mean aggregation; preference versus likelihood objectives; normalization; token count and steering strength; layer/token injection; and vision-only versus text-only variants.
The method is presented clearly with intuitive pipeline figures, qualitative examples, attribution heatmaps, runtime measurements, prompts, and implementation details that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental because GRAINS mainly combines existing components—Integrated Gradients, contrastive activation steering, PCA, and norm preservation. The paper should more sharply distinguish its causal claim from prior token-attribution and multimodal-steering work.

Statistical robustness is underdeveloped. There are no reported seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance across the 50 randomly sampled preference examples used to construct steering vectors. The hyperparameter curves and main tables appear to report single runs.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. In particular, 'without degrading fluency' is assessed using MMLU/MMMU and a nonstandard BLEU-based preference metric, not perplexity, human fluency evaluation, or open-ended generation quality. The reported percentage gains should also be labeled as percentage points where appropriate.

The claimed lowest hallucination rate is not uniform across every model: on Qwen-VL MMHal-Bench, LoRA achieves 0.461 versus 0.473 for GRAINS, although GRAINS has the best average. This should be stated more precisely.

There is an unexplained discrepancy between the Llama Toxigen base score in Table 1 (51.19) and Table 8 (48.10). If these use different splits, the tables must say so; otherwise this is an internal consistency problem.

Several implementation details needed for exact reproduction are unspecified, including the IG/masking baseline for text and visual tokens, how PCA component signs are oriented, whether activations are centered before PCA, and the exact teacher-forced target used when computing contrastive log-probability gradients. The code link also appears empty in the manuscript.

GPT-4o is used as the MMHal-Bench judge, with limited human validation, so judge bias and reliability remain possible concerns. Baseline adaptation, especially CAA for VLMs, should also be described more carefully to establish fairness.

The evaluation is concentrated on 7B/12B models, English safety tasks, and a single globally tuned steering strength. Robustness to multiple simultaneous attributes, larger models, and adaptive or instance-specific lambda values remains limited.
